newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: Papua New Guinea major says rebels control army.
newsitem.headline: Papua New Guinea major says rebels control army.

text.p: Rebel army officers in Papua New Guinea said on Saturday that they, not a commander appointed by the government, controlled the country's defence force.

As calm returned to the streets of the capital Port Moresby after two days of street violence, rebel officers again called on Prime Minister Sir Julius Chan to resign by next Tuesday, when parliament resumes ahead of June elections.
But rebel leader Major Walter Enuma said troops would take no action if Chan refused, saying only that public pressure could force him from office.
"The defence force does not intend to take any action. We have achieved our military aim, it's up to the public to demonstrate and keep the pressure on the politicians," he said.

Troops meanwhile handed former British colonel Tim Spicer over to police. Spicer led a group of around 70 mercenaries hired in a US$36 million contract to crush an uprising on copper-rich Bougainville island but forced out of this South Pacific nation by troops they were meant to have led.

A police spokesman said Spicer, a former top U.N. peacekeeper who also served in the Falkands and Gulf wars, would be questioned and could then be released. British diplomats in Port Moresby were waiting for him to be handed over to them.
Some 50 of Spicer's men were forced out of the country on Friday by Enuma, following others who left earlier in the week.

The PNG political crisis began on Monday when army commander Brigadier-General Jerry Singirok demanded Chan quit over his hiring of Spicer's mercenaries. He also demanded Spicer and his men be expelled before they could launch a Bougainville assault.
Singirok was promptly fired and replaced by Colonel Alfred Aikung, an army outsider, but retains the loyalty of his troops and officers.
"The acting commander does not have control of the defence force, the prime minister has been misled," Enuma told a news conference at army headquarters, Murray Barracks, on Saturday.
"The acting commander does not have the confidence of the troops. We are in command, we are in control," added Enuma, surrounded by armed troops.

Outside Murray Barracks, near the scene of violent street battles this week between civilian protesters and police loyal to Chan, Aikung's burnt-out car gave further proof he had no control of the army. Onlookers said soldiers torced the car.
The car was covered in angry notices. "Graduated from University of Pacific Engineering, majored in corruption, bribes, power-hungry and glory-seeking," said one. "Lest we forget, RIP," read another.
Enuma said Aikung was not under house arrest but was confined to barracks like the rest of the defence force.

Singirok's supporters, led by Enuma, have demanded that the former commander be given back his job. Singirok, a "soldier's soldier" who was injured trying to rescue a wounded comrade in Bougainville, is immensely popular among the army rank-and-file.

But the rebels appeared on Saturday to have softened their position on his reinstatement. Enuma said troops would return to normal duties if Singirok was reinstated or his chief of staff Colonel Jack Tuat was appointed acting commander.
The demand for Chan and two of his ministers to resign by Tuesday came initially from Singirok on Friday. He said the contract with Spicer's British mercenary firm was unlawful and unconstitutional.
The 10-page legal contract, marked "strictly confidential" and between Papua New Guinea and British-based mercenary firm Sandline International, was handed to reporters by Singirok.

It showed that the mainly South African veterans led by Spicer were not hired just to train troops but to conduct "offensive operations" to quell the Bougainville uprising and recapture a vast copper mine on the island.

The contract, signed by Deputy Prime Minister Chris Haiveta and Spicer, stipulated the mercenaries, described as "special constables", would "conduct offensive operations in Bougainville in conjunction with PNG defence forces to render the (Bougainville Revolutionary Army) militarily ineffective and repossess the Panguna mine".
Internationally condemned for hiring the mercenaries, Chan had said they would only be used to train PNG troops and would go to Bougainville only as consultants.
The contract stated the mercenaries would be employed for an initial period of three months or until the BRA were defeated.

An appendix broke down costs into $29 million for equipment and $7 million for manpower. The cost for a 45-strong "special forces team" was put at $4.5 million -- or $100,000 per soldier. PNG soldiers earn around $40 a week.
